paragraphs.text: All Scripture is inspired by God and profitable, for it has the Spirit of truth as the source and spring of its godliness. From the holy and adorable Spirit, as from a flourishing and fertile spring, all the divine streams flow. Whatever the law ordains, whatever the prophets declare, whatever the apostles preach, all of it is truly to be likened and ascribed to the Holy Spirit. For one and the same Spirit works all things, distributing to each one individually as he wills. That is why all the beauties of godliness flash out, the words of truth shine, and the treasures of divine wisdom pour forth. These treasures are not hidden away in the earth but are seen in the depths of godliness. They gladden souls, enlighten minds, turn the world back to God, and enrich all the poverty of Adam. When Adam stripped off the original beauty of godliness he was brought down into deep humiliation, and in the same way he was made rich through the condescension of God the Word, our Savior. Paul bears witness to this when he says somewhere: "I give thanks to God that in everything you were enriched in him, in all speech and all knowledge." Whoever receives the word of God is rich, and whoever does not receive the word of God is poor. Jeremiah bears witness to this too: "And I said, Perhaps they are poor; that is why they cannot hear the word of the Lord." But the poor man is reproached, while the rich man rejoices: the man who is rich in the word of truth and luxuriant with the virtues of a fruitful philosophy. David was such a man when he said, "I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God." He was a fruitful olive tree, not luxuriant with leaves but laden with the fruits of godliness. For a soul is often luxuriant with branches and leaves and yet bears no fruit, as Jeremiah said of Israel: "Israel is a vine rich in branches." It was rich in branches, not rich in fruit. That is what she was like. But the prophet rejoices and says, "I am like a fruitful olive tree," not luxuriant on the outside but teeming within, "a fruitful olive tree in the house of God." For it is not good to live outside the house of God.

You will find many people outside the word of truth who, to all appearances, shine with good works. You will find compassionate, merciful men devoted to justice. Yet their works bear no fruit, because they have not known the work of truth. Works are good, but the highest work must come first. Once the Jews said to the Lord, "What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?" and he answered them, "This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent." See how he called faith a work. So the moment you believed, you flourished with works at once. This is not because faith falls short when it comes to works, but because faith in itself is full of good works. Works are directed toward people and come from people, but faith goes from people to God. Faith makes the one who turns to God a citizen of heaven. Faith makes a person of earth a companion of God. Nothing outside faith is good. If I may use an image to illustrate my point, brothers, those who flourish with good works but do not know the God of godliness seem to me like the bodies of the dead: they are dressed in fine clothes but have no sense of their finery. What good is a dead soul, dead to God the Word yet clothed in good works? Works are done in the hope of reward and crowns. But if you do not know who presides over the contest, for whom are you competing? Faith must not be stripped of works, or it will be scorned. Still, faith ranks above works. Among human beings, life has to come first and then nourishment, since food is what sustains our life. In the same way, hope in Christ must come first in our life, and we must also be nourished by good works. Someone who is not fed can often go on living, but someone who is not alive cannot be fed. Moses fasted forty days, but because he had the living Word within him, the lack of earthly things did him no harm. It is the same with the state of the soul. It must be nourished by works, but before works it must put on faith. Without faith you cannot show me anyone who did works of righteousness and lived and was counted worthy of the kingdom. No one has lived without faith, but the thief was justified by believing alone. Do not tell me, "He had no time to live a virtuous life." I am not disputing that. What I have shown is that faith by itself saved him. If he had lived on after believing and neglected works, he would have fallen away from salvation. The point we are examining now is this: faith by itself has saved, but works by themselves have never justified those who did them. Do you want to see clearly that works without faith do not give life?

Cornelius had a good name for his almsgiving and prayers, but he did not know Christ. He believed in God but had not yet learned of God's Word. Because his works were good and wonderful, he pleased God, who loves good things and rewards them. But the great eye of righteousness and truth, the impartial and just Judge, saw that his works were good but dead, because they had no faith. So he sent a divine angel to reward the works and to crown the man who was competing well with faith. The angel said to him: "Cornelius, your prayers and your alms have gone up as a memorial before God." "If my petition has been heard," Cornelius in effect says, "and my alms have been accepted, what do I still lack for righteousness?" "Send to Joppa," the angel says, "and summon Simon who is called Peter. He will come and speak words to you by which you will be saved, you and all your household." So the works did not contain salvation. If he and his household are saved by what Peter preaches, then Cornelius did not yet have salvation from his works, until faith gave his works their prize. That is why Peter, the blessed and honored apostle of Christ, came from Joppa, saw the grace of God poured out on those who were then considered foreigners, and came to understand God's judgment. He said: "Truly I perceive that God shows no partiality, but in every nation whoever does righteousness is acceptable to him." He did not say, "In every nation whoever does righteousness is saved," but "is acceptable," that is, he becomes worthy of being received. So faith must shine out ahead of works, and works must follow faith. Let no one bring faith into disrepute by bearing no fruit, and let no one bring works into disrepute by unbelief. Become a fruitful olive tree, but in the house of God. Being a fruitful olive tree means good works. Being in the house of God points to faith.

What are the works of God? We all know them, if we are willing to do them, for nothing about them is hidden. Points of doctrine are disputed, but what concerns works is not hidden, because nature itself dictates the laws. We know of ourselves what is good and what is evil. God placed an unwritten law in nature to enlighten our minds. Let no one say, "I have not read the law; I do not know what the law requires." If you deny the common law, the law of nature convicts you. Do you want to learn that God set in nature the laws that tell good from evil? Look at our own way of life: everyone who does evil shrinks from being called by the name of that evil. Listen to how this works. The adulterer commits adultery, but he is ashamed when he hears himself called an adulterer. Call an admitted adulterer "Adulterer!" and he is ashamed to hear what he enjoys doing. Yet if you think the sin is good, why do you shrink from its name? Call a perjurer "Perjurer!" and he takes the name of his own deeds as an insult. So nature itself cries out that what is base is foreign to God's work. What God made is good, and very good. It is so good that even when it is mixed up in evil, it is ashamed of wickedness. Call a self-controlled man "Self-controlled!" and he is not ashamed even of the name of the deed he enjoys. Call a just man just, and he is crowned by the deed and takes pride in the name. Even if he declines the title out of reverence, in his soul he welcomes the praise.

Think how much wickedness goes about in the world without a face of its own. How can it have no face? If you look closely, you will find that no vice appears with a face of its own. Unless it borrows the face of virtue, it does not show itself. Listen to how this works. The liar does not lie by admitting that he is lying; he deceives by pretending to tell the truth. The wrongdoer does not announce what he is. He poses as what he is not, and then he does the wrong. In the same way the deceitful man does not show his deceit. He pretends to be a friend, and so carries out his villainy. The adulterer does not burst into a house after confessing his lawless adultery. He puts on a show of chastity and outrages divine things with his mouth [?]. Do you see that vice has no face of its own? The same is true of the false accuser. When he goes into court, he does not go in admitting what he is. He puts on the appearance of a witness to the truth, and through his lie he shows himself a witness for wickedness. So vice has no face of its own unless it borrows the face of virtue. That is why the Savior said: "They will come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves."
But let us return to our subject.

Brother, do you want to see how powerful the innate law is? Even when our soul is mixed up in vices, it embraces a good name. Many powerful men breathe greed and think of nothing but plunder and injustice. Yet often certain people persuade them to lift the burden pressing on a poor man, or to forgive part of a debt, or not to take revenge on those who have offended them or are thought to have offended them. A man who comes to plead skillfully with a powerful and wicked man does not begin straight away with the truth. He does not tell him what he is. Instead, he gives him the name of virtue. Do you not know how skilled pleaders always put on a manner? "You are a good man," he says. "Your name is famous everywhere, and everyone sings of your good deeds." He adds many things like this to his plea, so that the man will be swayed by the praise and turn away from wickedness. See how vice is overcome by the praises of virtue. No wicked man wants to be called wicked. Nature embraces what belongs to it, even when the will chooses the opposite.

So let us become a fruitful olive tree, beloved, flourishing with works and fruit and leaves. Our leaves are our words, and our fruit is our way of life. Let your speech be dignified and your way of life fruitful. In a godly man, not even the leaf is to be thrown away. "His leaf," says David, "shall not fall, and whatever he does shall prosper." But how wonderful this is! I have thought about how Adam went out of paradise naked, and how David flourishes in the house of God. Adam went out naked because of his transgression. David, clothed in virtues, cries out, "But I am like a fruitful olive tree." Nothing strips us bare like fruitlessness, and nothing clothes us like bearing fruit through good works. Adam was formed... But I must now repeat what has already been said, since repeating good things fixes teaching firmly in our souls. When wool is dyed, it is dipped in the dye again and again so that the dye can do its work deep inside. In the same way our souls must be dipped again and again in the divine words, so that the old disgrace may be washed away and we may put on the new beauty. Once that wool has taken the dye, it lays aside the name of its nature and takes the name of the dye. You no longer call it wool but purple, or scarlet, or green, or whatever beauty the dye has given it. If dye changes the name of a nature, does not God's nature change a human being? Before the dyeing the same person is an earthly image; after it he is a radiant, heavenly image. Adam, then, was formed poor from the earth, for God took dust and formed him. But as I said before, Adam did not see how he was formed. He was not to be present as a witness of what was being done, lest he exalt himself against God. Clothed in such lowliness, he still exalts himself, ignores his Creator, and rejects the one who formed him. If he had received something beyond his nature, who could have endured his boundless arrogance? That is why, when God formed man, he placed in his creature both great powers and many humiliations. The power within it was meant to make people admire the Craftsman's grace, and the humiliation was meant to check human pride. He gave him a tongue that speaks, praises God, sings of divine things, and puts the beauties of creation into words. The tongue, a little scrap of flesh not even two fingers long, discourses about heaven and earth. Why do I say fingers? It is not even the tip of a fingernail, and yet that little, paltry tip speaks of heaven and earth. So that it will not think itself something great and exalt itself beyond its own nature, it is often afflicted with growths and sores. This teaches it that, though mortal, it speaks of things eternal and immortal, and that it should recognize the power of the one it proclaims and the weakness of the one who proclaims. He gave him an eye, that little millet seed. It is the center that sees, the very middle of the pupil. Yet through that little millet seed he looks upon the whole creation. So that he will not exalt himself because his sight takes in the whole creation, inflammations, discharges, tears, and everything that clouds the sight often arise. Through this weakness he comes to know himself, and through the workmanship he glorifies the Craftsman as divine. He gave him a heart that reasons, the root of intentions and the spring of thoughts. But in that very region God also formed the intestines, which are filled with dung and every other kind of filth from what a person eats. So when the heart exalts itself, the belly humbles it, and both the belly and the dung are necessary to train us. A man who carries dung around with him dares to be insolent. Nor is he merely insolent; he is insolent even against God, as a certain barbarian king dared to say: "I will set my throne above the stars, and I will be like the Most High." If he talks like this while carrying around so much dung and filth, who could have endured his self-exaltation if he had been entirely free of this weakness and lowliness? That is why the great Isaiah says to the proud: "Why are earth and ashes arrogant?"
But let us return again to our subject.

God created humankind from dust. But the man did not see how he came into being, and so he did not know how lowly he was. For God, as I said before, did not make the soul before the body, so that it would not watch its own making. But since the man had no idea at all how low a state he had been raised from, or that the Creator had formed him from the earth, God sends him back to the earth from which he was taken. In this way, having learned his own weakness by experience, he may come to know both the kindness God showed him at the beginning and the love for humankind that is still to come. When he was formed, he did not see that he came from the earth. Pay close attention, so that the meaning does not slip past you. When Adam was being formed, he did not see that he rose up from earth. But when he is raised in the resurrection, he sees that he rises having shed the dust. For even if a dead man does not see himself, he sees the one who died before him. We see those who have died and turned to dust, and what we see teaches us. Have you not often seen bold and arrogant men become humble and subdued when someone dies? A death is announced, and every heart cowers and all pride sinks. And we philosophize at the tombs. When we see bare bones and consider human nature eaten away and fallen apart, at once we philosophize to one another: "See what we become, and where we are going." Yet it is all idle talk. We leave the tombs and forget how lowly we are. At the tomb each one says something like this to his neighbor: "Oh, the misery of it! Oh, how pitiable our life is! See what we become!" And yet even while we say it, we grab at things, we shout, and we hold grudges. Each one philosophizes as if he were about to renounce wickedness completely. Inside he philosophizes in words, but outside he fights against God in his deeds. This is why God arranged for tombs to be set up everywhere, to remind us of our own weakness. That is why every city and every village has tombs in front of its gates. A man hurries to enter a royal city, splendid with wealth and power and every other distinction. Before he sees what he imagines, he first sees what we all become. There are tombs in front of the cities and tombs in front of the fields. Everywhere the school of our lowliness is set before us. We are taught first where we end up, and only then do we see the illusions inside. And that is not all. Often, when we are about to enter the partnership of married life, we are taught the utter lowliness of our nature. A man who wants to take a wife often dictates the terms of the dowry to the notary. There is no union yet, and already death is written down. He has not yet enjoyed living together in marriage, and at once he makes provision for death. He has not yet seen his bride, and he sets down sentences of death in advance against himself and against her. He writes things like this: "If the husband dies before the wife, or the wife before the husband, such and such is stipulated." So the ancient laws planted reminders of our nature everywhere, for everyone. The sentences of death are laid down not only for those who exist and are alive, but even for those not yet born. For what does the document say? "And if the child to be born should die." The fruit does not exist yet, and the sentence has already run ahead of it. So in his documents he acknowledges nature: "If anything of the human lot should befall." But if his wife actually dies, he forgets what he wrote and speaks other words, words fit for a tragedy: "Did I have to suffer this? Did I ever expect to suffer this and lose my wife?" What then? Have you forgotten what you wrote? When you stood outside these events, you recognized the limits of nature. Now that you have fallen into suffering, have you forgotten the laws of nature? These things are said to correct us all, so that all of us may bear nobly whatever befalls us and not count God's judgments as a loss. Do not philosophize only when you are free of suffering. When you are in the midst of suffering, show your greatness of soul. When you grieve, remember the words you use to comfort the grieving. What words do we use with those who grieve? Do we not philosophize to them like this? "These misfortunes are part of human life. You are not the only one to suffer misfortune. You are not the only one to endure the violence of death. Kings bear these things too. Rulers have often suffered loss, and the powerful suffer loss as well. Know your own nature: you are a human being. You too, along with everyone else, share in the common laws of nature."

You say these things, and more, when you comfort someone else. Are you a fine teacher for others, but for yourself not even a poor pupil? It takes a great and noble soul to philosophize when suffering is at its height. If anyone can say, at every misfortune or grief or loss, "You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgments are upright," he suffers loss as a human being but is crowned as one who loves God. Life, brothers, is full of hardship, and the righteous and the unrighteous, the pious and the impious, must all be afflicted. But the difference is great. It is one thing to be disciplined as a member of the household, and another to be flogged as a stranger. A son is beaten, and a servant is beaten. But the servant is beaten as a slave who has done wrong, and the son as one who is free, a son who needs correcting. The blows do not make them equal in rank. If a pious man suffers what an impious man suffers, that does not make him equal in rank with the impious. For him the discipline counts as affliction and testing. For the impious it counts as flogging and punishment. That is why the blessed David, knowing these hardships, says of the righteous: "Many are the afflictions of the righteous." But see what follows: "And the Lord will deliver them out of them all." Of the opposite kind he says: "Many are the scourges of the sinner," and nothing follows. The afflictions of the righteous are many, but the Lord will deliver them out of them all. Let no one who hears this despair of himself or say: "If I am scourged as a sinner and have no hope, then my discipline bears no fruit for me." Here scripture calls a sinner not someone wholly estranged from piety, but someone who is afflicted, who has a share in piety but slips in human affairs. For all of scripture is full of pledges of God's love for humankind, showing that God has mercy on sinners. It says: "As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live." God swears an oath, not because he distrusts himself, but to force our unbelief into faith. So let every person who is tested by afflictions say: "You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgments are upright." In saying it he shows a noble soul and also keeps his piety unbroken.

Such was the blessed Job. He led the fight against every suffering, overcame every terror the devil could devise, broke all the devil's fury, and by his firm resolve scattered the devil's waves. He was stripped of everything at once, yet he did not deny the Lord of all. But his feats of generalship will get a discourse of their own. They truly need their own occasion to be examined, so that we do not insult his struggles by hurrying past them. For now, let us keep before our eyes what that noble and great champion said. When he set a seal on what had been said, stripped of everything as he was but not stripped of his piety, he said: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away. As it seemed good to the Lord, so it has come to pass." "Seemed good" is well said. He yields to God's authority. He does not pry into God's governance. He did not say, as we do: "Why do the young die and the old live on? What sort of governance is this? An old man longs for death. His flesh is worn out, he lacks money and every other comfort, yet he does not get what he longs for. Meanwhile a child of lovely beauty, dear to its parents, is snatched away before its time?" Learn not to ask such things. Learn to say: "Your judgments are a great deep." Learn to say: "You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgments are upright." Learn to say: "As it seemed good to the Lord, so it has come to pass." Acknowledge his authority, so that you may come to know piety.

But since our discourse has fallen upon the glory of the Holy Spirit, let us also say something about doctrine, for our own safety and confirmation. When Job said, "As it seemed good to the Lord," he showed God's authority and lordship. In the same way the apostles showed the sovereign authority of the Holy Spirit when they said: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit to lay on you nothing beyond what is necessary." "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit." If he is a subject, why did it "seem good" to him? If the Spirit is under laws and serves, how can something "seem good" to one who is subject? Is it not what seems good to the king that comes to pass, rather than what occurs to his subjects? "As it seemed good to the Lord," says Job. "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit," say the apostles. The language of authority is equal in honor, since the glory of the kingdom is undivided. But here again the wickedness of the heretics finds a way to slip in. "The apostles said, 'It seemed good to the Holy Spirit,'" they say, "but they added 'and to us.' Does that give the apostles the authority of divinity?" These matters must be studied, so that the heretics do not inject the venom of their disobedience into untrained souls or pour heretical impiety into the ears of the guileless. For they often speak in solemn tones like this: "Brother," one says, "do not be surprised by anything that has been said." He calls you brother and kills you as an enemy. "Do not marvel," he says, "that the apostles said of the Holy Spirit, 'It seemed good to the Holy Spirit.' Look at what follows too: 'It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.' It seemed good to the apostles. Are the apostles gods, then? Do they have God's authority?" When the heretic says these things, let us bring out arrows from holy scripture. For "the arrows of the Mighty One are sharpened, sent into the heart of the king's enemies." What, then, can we say to him? If being joined with the apostles lowers the dignity of the Holy Spirit, then being joined with Moses lowers the dignity of God. Here is what I mean. If you do not think "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit" is a great thing because the apostles are joined to it, then you cannot call faith in God a great thing either, because Moses is joined to God as well. For scripture says: "The people believed in God and in Moses." Let us bring out another arrow too. If the glory of the apostles, joined to the Spirit, pulls down the Spirit's dignity, then Samuel, added alongside God, insults God and lowers his glory. For it is written: "And all the people feared the Lord and Samuel." Let us bring yet a third arrow against this impiety. If being joined with the apostles lowers the dignity and divine authority of the Holy Spirit, then Gideon, added to God's name, lowers God's dignity too. For all the people cried out in battle: "A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!" Moses is joined to God not as God's equal in honor but as God's servant. Samuel is joined to God not as his equal but as a prophet. Gideon is joined to God not as his equal but as the general in the war. In the same way the apostles are joined to the Spirit as heralds of the gospel. So acknowledge his authority, and do not insult the dignity of the Spirit. Acknowledge the divine teaching about the Holy Trinity, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. This is the uncreated nature, the true dignity, the undivided kingdom, the unsplit honor, the indivisible hope, the incomprehensible glory of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. To him belong all glory, honor and worship, to the ages of ages. Amen.
